seo.title: Web design process: how a project runs
seo.description: The five stages of a Calwebtech project, from discovery to handover: what happens each week, what you receive and what we need from your team.

hero.title: How a website project runs
hero.answer: A Calwebtech project runs in five stages: discovery, design, build, prove and launch. A marketing site takes six to eight weeks from start to handover and a platform build nine to fourteen, with the price fixed in writing in the first week. Each stage below lists what you get and what we need from you, because most projects stall on content, not code.
hero.intro: Published in full, including what we need from you and when. The dates are shared dates: we hold ours, and the plan shows exactly where yours fall.

steps.heading: What happens at each stage of a project?
steps.intro: Five stages, each with a clear output. From the build stage onwards there is a staging site you can open on any day.
steps.empty: The stages of our process are being updated. Ask us and we will walk you through how your project would run.

principles.heading: Why does the timeline hold?
principles.intro: Schedules slip when decisions are left open. These habits close them early.

items.title: The price is fixed before design starts
items.body: Scope, timeline and exclusions are agreed in writing in the first week, so nobody discovers the real budget halfway through the build.

items.title: Patterns before pages
items.body: Design tokens and a component library come first. Most pages are then assembled from approved patterns, which is why design takes two weeks rather than two months.

items.title: Work happens in the open
items.body: A staging URL you can open any day, a weekly progress call and early access to the dashboard. Nothing only works on a demo day.

items.title: The people in the pitch build it
items.body: Senior people stay on your project from discovery to handover. There is no handover to a junior team after the contract is signed.

delays.heading: What usually slows a website project down?
delays.intro: The cause is rarely code. These are the delays we plan around from the first week.

items.title: Content arriving late
items.body: Copy, product data and images are the most common blocker. The plan names the date each piece is needed, and we can draft copy for your approval if writing is the bottleneck.

items.title: Feedback spread across people
items.body: Five sets of comments that contradict each other cost a week. We ask for one consolidated review per stage from a named decision maker.

items.title: Waiting for integration access
items.body: API keys, test accounts and documentation for your CRM or ERP take time to arrange internally. We ask for them in discovery so they are ready for the build.

items.title: Legal sign-off left to the end
items.body: Privacy policies, terms and regulated claims need approval before launch. We flag them in week one so approval never holds up the cutover.

afterLaunch.heading: What happens after launch?
afterLaunch.body: Launch is the start of the site’s working life, not the end of the project. For 60 days anything that does not behave as specified is fixed free, with a four hour response on critical issues, and after that you decide whether to keep us on.

faq.heading: What else do people ask about the process?
faq.intro: Timelines, working alongside your existing developer and what we need from you.

cta.heading: Ready to see how your project would run?
cta.body: Tell us what you need. We reply within one business day and map the five stages onto your own dates on a thirty minute call.

steps.title: Discovery
steps.summary: Positioning, audience, service catalogue, sitemap and a conversion map for every page.
steps.heading: We work out what is actually wrong
steps.body: A working session on positioning, buyers and the service catalogue. We map the primary action for every page and agree the sitemap before anyone opens a design tool.

image.alt: Discovery workshop with the client team

steps.title: Design
steps.summary: Tokens, component library and high-fidelity screens for the pages that carry the money.
steps.heading: You see real screens, not a mood board
steps.body: Design tokens and a component library first, then high-fidelity screens for the pages that carry the money. Everything else is assembled from approved patterns, which is why this stage does not drag.

steps.title: Build
steps.summary: Front end, API, dashboard and integrations, reviewed on a staging URL you can open any day.
steps.heading: A staging URL you can open any day
steps.body: Front end, API, dashboard and integrations, built in the open. Weekly progress notes, no black box, and nothing that only works on a demo day.

steps.title: Prove
steps.summary: Cross-browser QA, accessibility audit, performance pass and a tested backup restore.
steps.heading: We try to break it before your customers do
steps.body: Cross-browser and cross-device QA, an accessibility audit, a performance pass against the written budget, structured data validation, redirect verification, and one tested backup restore.
youGet: A restore proven in front of you
weNeed: A test run of your own

image.alt: Performance and analytics review before launch

steps.title: Launch
steps.summary: DNS cutover, monitoring, two training sessions and the full documentation set.
steps.heading: You leave owning all of it
steps.body: DNS cutover, monitoring switched on, two recorded training sessions, a written operations manual, and every account transferred into your name through a password manager.

image.alt: Handover and training session with the client team

faqs.question: How long does a project take?
faqs.answer: Six to eight weeks for a marketing site, nine to fourteen for a platform build with booking, a dashboard and integrations. The most common cause of delay is content, not code, which is why the proposal names the dates we need things from you.

faqs.question: What if we already have a developer?
faqs.answer: That is common and usually fine. We can take design and front end and leave the back end with your team, or work the other way round. The proposal will say exactly where the boundary sits so nobody is guessing.

faqs.question: What do you need from us during a project?
faqs.answer: A named decision maker, about ninety minutes of your team in discovery, your brand assets and service list, and feedback on designs within two days. Content is the most common cause of delay, so the proposal names the dates we need copy, images and integration credentials.

faqs.question: What happens after I get in touch?
faqs.answer: We read your message, look at your current site and email you within one business day to book a thirty minute call. After that call you get a written proposal with scope, timeline and a fixed price within two business days. If we are not the right fit we will say so and point you somewhere better.
